questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Approving a new data use
questions.question: A grocery chain's analytics team asks a risk practitioner about copying loyalty-card purchase records into a new reporting tool. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate approver for this new use?

options.A: The business manager accountable for the customer records
options.B: The risk analyst who assessed the reporting tool's security
options.C: The CISO, who sets the organization's data security policy
options.D: The IT manager who runs the database for the business

questions.key_concept: The data owner, an accountable business manager, approves access to and new uses of data; IT is the custodian.
questions.pre_read: For each person named, ask what their role lets them decide about the data.
questions.correct_explanation: The data owner, the business manager accountable for the customer records, sets the rules for using the data. They can judge whether the reporting use fits the purpose the data was collected for and its classification. The CISO sets security policy and advises on controls, but does not own business data or decide its uses; the IT manager is the custodian who carries out the owner's rules.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the analyst knows the tool's risks. But the analyst assesses and advises; approving a new use of business data is the data owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the CISO sets security policy and can advise on controls. But policy authority is not data ownership; the accountable business manager approves uses.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because IT runs the database. But IT is the custodian: it applies the owner's rules and cannot judge the data's business value or permitted uses.

tips: Eliminate: D names the custodian, who carries out the owner's rules, and B names the risk analyst, who advises but does not approve uses of business data.
Final two: A beats C because data ownership sits with the accountable business manager; the CISO sets security policy but does not decide business uses.
Exam cue: who decides access, use or retention of data? The data owner, a business role, not IT, security or the risk function.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (data owner); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Information Owner/Steward)

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Investment prioritization
questions.question: A hospital's investment committee must choose between two projects with similar returns. One project retires a system tied to a high-rated patient-safety risk. Which of the following inputs from the risk practitioner is MOST useful?

options.A: Each project manager's own project risk log
options.B: A ranking of the projects by return on investment
options.C: A new rating of the patient-safety risk against appetite
options.D: Each project's effect on the enterprise risk profile

questions.key_concept: Portfolio decisions weigh value and risk together, including the enterprise risk a project would reduce.
questions.pre_read: Note what the two projects share and what separates them, then ask which information shows that difference.
questions.correct_explanation: With returns roughly equal, the deciding difference is risk. Showing how each project would change the enterprise risk profile, including the patient-safety risk one would reduce, lets the committee weigh value and risk together and make the call. Re-rating the patient-safety risk, already rated high, sizes one effect but misses any risk the other project would reduce or add, so it cannot settle the comparison.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because project teams know their own risks. But project logs track delivery risks such as delay and overrun, not how each choice changes the enterprise's exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because return is the usual basis for investment. But it cannot separate two projects with similar returns, and it hides the risk reduction one of them offers.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it sizes the risk one project would retire. But the committee is comparing two projects, so it needs each one's effect on the whole risk profile.

tips: Eliminate: B ranks on return, which cannot separate projects with similar returns, and A offers project delivery logs that do not show enterprise exposure.
Final two: D beats C because the committee is choosing between two projects; rating one risk alone misses what else each project adds or removes.
Exam cue: in portfolio items, the practitioner gives decision-makers value and risk together, including risks a project would reduce; the committee decides.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Ransomware restore sequence
questions.question: Ransomware has encrypted a distributor's order system, and the operations director urges an immediate restore from last night's backup to resume shipping. What should the risk practitioner advise FIRST?

options.A: Restore the order system from last night's backup
options.B: Contain the attack before the order system is restored
options.C: Pay the ransom if it costs less than the outage losses
options.D: Restore from an older backup made before the attack began

questions.key_concept: During ransomware recovery, contain the attack first, then verify the backup is clean before restoring.
questions.pre_read: Notice the pressure in the stem and what is still unknown about the attack.
questions.correct_explanation: Restoring while the attacker still has access, or from a backup that holds the malware, invites a second encryption and a longer outage. Containment comes first; the backup is then verified as clean, and only then is the system restored. An older backup lowers the chance of restoring malware, but without containment the attacker can simply encrypt the restored system again, and an older copy also loses more orders.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is fastest. But if the attacker is still inside or the backup carries the malware, the restored system is encrypted again.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it may look like the quickest way back. But paying is a senior management and legal decision, does not guarantee recovery and may breach sanctions rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: an older copy is less likely to hold malware. But without containment the attacker can re-encrypt it, and it loses more data.

tips: Eliminate: A restores into a live attack, and C reduces a legal and senior management decision about paying criminals to a cost comparison.
Final two: B beats D because containment must come first; an older backup restored without containment can be encrypted again and costs extra lost data.
Exam cue: in ransomware recovery the order is contain, verify the backup is clean, then restore; the practitioner advises on that order, and the incident lead and business owner decide.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Framework alignment and ratings
questions.question: A bank's latest framework assessment shows its cybersecurity practices meet the target profile, and the CIO proposes lowering every cyber risk rating in the register by one level. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Lower the ratings, taking the assessment as evidence
options.B: Lower the ratings for scenarios the improved practices address
options.C: Convert the profile's outcome scores into new risk ratings
options.D: Reassess each scenario on evidence before changing its rating

questions.key_concept: Framework alignment is evidence about controls; a risk rating changes only when the scenario's likelihood and impact are reassessed.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a framework profile measures and what a risk rating measures.
questions.correct_explanation: A profile shows which framework outcomes the bank achieves; it does not measure the likelihood and impact of each risk scenario. A register rating records current risk, so it changes only when that scenario is reassessed on evidence such as control test results, threats and impacts. Lowering the ratings for scenarios the improved practices address is closer, but it still moves ratings on alignment, not on each scenario's reassessment.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the assessment is recent and favorable. But profiles describe outcomes achieved, not exposure; a bank can meet its target profile and still face scenarios rated high.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it targets the scenarios the practices touch. But it still lowers ratings on alignment alone; without evidence of the effect on likelihood or impact, no rating should move.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the scores are recent and structured. But they show which practices the bank achieves, not any scenario's likelihood or impact; converting them skips the reassessment they should inform.

tips: Eliminate: A treats framework alignment as proof of lower risk, and C turns outcome scores, which measure practices achieved, straight into ratings.
Final two: D beats B because a rating reflects a scenario's likelihood and impact; matching practices to scenarios is not evidence that either has changed.
Exam cue: framework alignment and certification are evidence about controls; a risk rating changes only when its scenario is reassessed.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. New use of customer data
questions.question: A retailer collects purchase history for its loyalty program, encrypts it and restricts access. Marketing now wants to infer customers' health conditions from that history for ads. What PRIMARY concern should the risk practitioner raise?

options.A: The encryption keys become a target for attackers
options.B: Marketing staff gain access to more customer records
options.C: Customer access requests extend to the inferred health data
options.D: The new use goes beyond the original collection purpose

questions.key_concept: Privacy governs whether a use of personal data fits its stated purpose; security only protects the data from unauthorized access.
questions.pre_read: Note what the retailer already does well, then ask what the new proposal changes.
questions.correct_explanation: Purpose limitation means personal data is collected for stated purposes and not used later in ways incompatible with them. Inferring health conditions from purchases for ads is a new and sensitive purpose customers never agreed to, whatever the encryption. Strong security keeps outsiders out but does not make an unfair use by authorized staff acceptable. Access requests are a real privacy right, but they follow from the use; they are not its main problem.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because keys guard the whole data set. But key theft is a security risk that existing controls address; the proposal raises how authorized staff will use the data.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because wider access raises exposure. But access can be limited to what the campaign needs; the deeper problem is whether this use is allowed at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: customers' right of access covers inferred data, a real privacy point. But it follows from the use; the problem is a sensitive new purpose customers never agreed to.

tips: Eliminate: A is a security concern about data that is already well protected, and B is about access scope; neither asks whether the new use is permitted.
Final two: D beats C because the proposal creates a new, sensitive use beyond the stated purpose; access requests follow from that use and are not its main problem.
Exam cue: privacy asks whether a use is fair and fits the stated purpose; strong encryption never answers that question.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Rising emergency changes
questions.question: Emergency changes at an online retailer rose from 5% to 30% of all changes in six months. The on-call manager approves each, and each is reviewed afterward. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A second approver for each emergency change request
options.B: Analysis of why changes are routed as emergencies
options.C: More frequent change board meetings for normal changes
options.D: Reporting of emergency change volume to senior management

questions.key_concept: A growing share of emergency changes signals the normal change path is being avoided; analyze why before adding approvals.
questions.pre_read: Notice which part of the emergency process works and what has changed.
questions.correct_explanation: A rise from 5% to 30% means the emergency route has become a normal path, and each case skips the full impact assessment and testing that normal changes get. The reviews afterward work, so the useful question is why teams use the route: slow approvals, poor planning or a way around scrutiny. Analyzing the cause lets the change manager fix it. More frequent board meetings guess at one cause.

wrong_explanations.A: A second approver tightens each emergency change; however, it adds weight to a path that should be rare and leaves the reason for the sixfold rise untouched.
wrong_explanations.C: Quicker approvals could help if delay is the cause; however, that is a guess until the reasons for the rise are analyzed.
wrong_explanations.D: Reporting keeps leaders informed of the trend; however, counting emergency changes does not explain why they rose or how to bring them down.

tips: Eliminate: A strengthens approval on a path whose after-the-fact reviews already work, and D keeps counting the rise without explaining it.
Final two: B beats C because the cause of the rise is not yet known; more frequent board meetings fix one guessed cause.
Exam cue: when a control's exception path becomes routine, find out why before adding steps; the volume is a symptom, not the cause.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Retrained model with unknown training data
questions.question: Monitoring showed a water utility's leak-prediction model got worse after retraining, and the data team cannot tell which data set trained it. Which of the following gaps does this MOST directly reveal?

options.A: No record linking model versions to training data
options.B: No fixed schedule for retraining the model
options.C: Weak access control over the training data store
options.D: No human review of the model's leak predictions

questions.key_concept: AI training data needs lineage: each model version is linked to the exact data that trained it, so faults can be traced and versions compared.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the stem states as fact from what might have caused the problem.
questions.correct_explanation: The stem gives one hard fact: nobody can say which data set trained the live model. That is a missing lineage record, which links each model version to the exact data used, so the team cannot trace the fault, compare versions or roll back with confidence. Weak access control is the runner-up: tampering could explain a worse model, but the stem gives no sign of it, while the missing record is certain.

wrong_explanations.B: A retraining schedule controls when models are refreshed; however, the problem here is not timing but that nobody can trace which data produced the live version.
wrong_explanations.C: Tampering with training data can degrade a model; however, nothing in the stem points to it, and any investigation first needs to know which data was used.
wrong_explanations.D: Human review can catch bad predictions; however, it oversees outputs and would not tell the team which data produced the worse model.

tips: Eliminate: B concerns when retraining happens, not what it used, and D reviews outputs without showing which data trained the model.
Final two: A beats C because the stem states the lineage gap as fact; tampering is a possible cause the stem gives no sign of.
Exam cue: for MOST directly, pick the gap the stem's facts prove, not one that might explain the event; training data needs lineage to each model version.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Releasing de-identified trip data
questions.question: A transit authority's data team will publish trip records that give each card one fixed random code and keep exact times and stops. What is the GREATEST privacy risk the risk practitioner should raise?

options.A: Decrypting the codes back into the card numbers
options.B: Errors in the trip data that mislead outside researchers
options.C: Linking each code's travel pattern to a known person
options.D: Authority staff misusing the records once published

questions.key_concept: De-identified records can be re-identified by linking what remains, such as exact times and places, to known people.
questions.pre_read: Look at what the authority keeps in the records, not only what it removes.
questions.correct_explanation: Replacing card numbers does not make data anonymous when each code follows one person and exact times and stops remain. A few known trips, such as a home stop at a regular hour, can tie a code to a person and expose all their travel. Decrypting the codes is the runner-up: random replacement values have no key to break, so the real exposure is linkage, not decryption.

wrong_explanations.A: Weak pseudonyms can sometimes be reversed; however, these codes are random replacements, not encrypted card numbers, so there is nothing to decrypt.
wrong_explanations.B: Data quality matters for research; however, errors mislead users of the data, while the privacy question is whether people can be identified.
wrong_explanations.D: Insider misuse is a real concern; however, once published the records are open to everyone, so staff access adds little to the exposure.

tips: Eliminate: B is a data quality concern, not a privacy one, and D worries about insiders when the data will be public.
Final two: C beats A because random codes cannot be decrypted, but a stable code with exact times and stops can be linked to a person.
Exam cue: de-identified data can still be re-identified; look at what remains, such as exact times, places or rare details, not just what was removed.

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Executives exempt from a control
questions.question: In a property developer's staff survey, most respondents say security rules feel optional because senior executives were exempted from the new sign-in checks. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A refresher security course for the whole staff
options.B: Disciplinary action for staff who bypass the sign-in checks
options.C: Executives using the same sign-in checks as their staff
options.D: A message from the CEO on why security rules matter

questions.key_concept: Tone at the top is set by leaders' actions; leaders exempt from a control signal that the control does not matter.
questions.pre_read: Notice why staff say the rules feel optional, then ask which option removes that reason.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff are reading the exemption as the real message: if leaders skip a control, the control must not matter. Culture follows what leaders do, so the fix is for executives to use the same checks. A message from the CEO is the runner-up; it sets the right words, but while the exemption stands, staff will believe the behavior rather than the message.

wrong_explanations.A: Staff already know the rules; the survey says they doubt them because of the exemption, which more training does not change.
wrong_explanations.B: Punishing staff treats a culture signal as misconduct and leaves in place the exemption that caused the doubt.
wrong_explanations.D: A CEO message answers a signal that was sent in words; here the signal is an exemption, and staff will weigh any message against what the executives visibly do.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains staff who already know the rules, and B punishes staff for a doubt that leaders created.
Final two: C beats D because tone at the top is set by what leaders do; a message cannot outweigh a visible exemption.
Exam cue: when a culture problem traces to leaders' own behavior, the BEST fix changes that behavior rather than training staff.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Logging that differs by team
questions.question: Incident reviews at a telecom found that each of its 30 product teams designs its own logging, and two customer apps kept no sign-in records. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Sign-in logging added to the two apps that lack it
options.B: A logging standard set in the enterprise architecture
options.C: A logging check in each product owner's go-live review
options.D: Each product owner's acceptance of their app's logging gaps

questions.key_concept: Security requirements set in the enterprise architecture are inherited by every new design, so a gap shared by many teams is fixed at that level.
questions.pre_read: Read both findings of the incident reviews before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Logging differs by team because nothing above the teams sets what must be logged, so new apps can repeat the gaps. A logging standard in the enterprise architecture defines the events every design records, so teams build it in and the two apps are brought up to it. A go-live check is the runner-up; it needs a standard to check against and catches gaps late, one app at a time, after each design is settled.

wrong_explanations.A: Adding sign-in logs fixes the two apps found so far; the other teams keep designing their own logging, so new gaps keep appearing.
wrong_explanations.C: A go-live check finds gaps when they are costliest to fix and still lets 30 teams design logging their own way.
wrong_explanations.D: Owner acceptance leaves the cause in place, and gaps that weaken incident investigations across the telecom are not one product team's decision.

tips: Eliminate: A patches the two apps found so far, and D has each product owner accept gaps whose cause sits above any one team.
Final two: B beats C because a requirement set in the architecture is built into every design; a go-live check finds gaps late, one app at a time.
Exam cue: when the same control gap appears across many teams' systems, look for the architecture standard that would build the control into every design.

options.A: Key developers may leave before the build is finished
options.B: The new system may go live with a weak access control
options.C: Errors in migrated records may carry into live payroll
options.D: The hosting vendor may miss its uptime target after launch

questions.key_concept: A project log holds delivery risks that end with the project; risks that continue into operation, or threaten enterprise objectives, go to the enterprise register.
questions.pre_read: Picture each risk happening, then note who would feel its effect and when.
questions.correct_explanation: A project log holds risks to delivery, which end when the project closes; developers leaving threatens the schedule and cost, then stops mattering. Risks whose effects continue in operation, or that threaten enterprise objectives, go to the enterprise register with an owner. Errors in migrated records are the runner-up; migration happens in the project, but wrong pay would keep reaching staff after go-live, so that risk outlasts the project.

wrong_explanations.B: A weak access control remains after go-live, so the risk outlasts the project and belongs with an operational owner in the enterprise register.
wrong_explanations.C: Migration happens during the project, but bad records would keep producing wrong pay after launch, so the risk reaches operations.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor uptime is an operating risk from launch onward; it belongs in the enterprise register with the payroll process owner.

tips: Eliminate: B and D describe the system in use after launch, so both risks outlast the project and need an operational owner.
Final two: A beats C because developer turnover ends with delivery; migration errors start in the project but keep affecting pay afterward.
Exam cue: ask whether a risk's effect ends at project closure; if it continues into operation, or could threaten enterprise objectives, it belongs in the enterprise register.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Standby vendor for an AI service
questions.question: A clinic's medical director adopted an AI scribe that saves doctors an hour daily. Outages are covered by typing and cost $10,000 yearly, within appetite. A standby vendor costs $90,000 yearly. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: A standby contract with a second AI scribe vendor
options.B: The medical director's recorded acceptance of the risk
options.C: Removal of the outage risk entry from the register
options.D: The medical director's withdrawal of the AI scribe tool

questions.key_concept: When the risk is within appetite and more recovery capacity costs more than the loss it prevents, the owner accepts on record and monitors.
questions.pre_read: Weigh the figures in the stem before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The standby vendor would cost $90,000 a year to prevent $10,000 of loss that is within appetite and limited by typing, so more treatment does not pay. The proportionate response is acceptance by the medical director, who adopted the scribe, recorded with a review date and monitored in case outages grow. Withdrawing the scribe is the runner-up; it ends the outage risk but gives up an hour a day per doctor for a small loss.

wrong_explanations.A: A standby vendor would cost $90,000 a year to prevent about $10,000 of loss; spending nine times the benefit is not a proportionate treatment.
wrong_explanations.C: An accepted risk stays in the register with its owner and is monitored; removing it means nobody would notice if the vendor's outages grew.
wrong_explanations.D: Withdrawal ends the outage risk, but it gives up an hour a day per doctor to avoid a small loss that the typing fallback already limits.

tips: Eliminate: A spends $90,000 a year to prevent $10,000 of loss, and C drops a risk from the register although accepted risks stay recorded and monitored.
Final two: B beats D because the scribe earns its keep and the loss is small; avoidance gives up that benefit, while acceptance keeps it.
Exam cue: within appetite, when treatment costs more than the loss it prevents and the technology earns its keep, expect the owner's recorded acceptance, with monitoring.

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. What a privacy impact assessment rates
questions.question: A dating service's privacy impact assessment covers a feature showing members' location to their matches. It rates each risk only by the fines and press coverage the service would face. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Fine estimates updated from recent enforcement cases
options.B: A penetration test of the feature before launch
options.C: Ratings that also count members who leave the service
options.D: Ratings that start from the harm that members could suffer

questions.key_concept: A privacy impact assessment rates the problems processing could cause people first, then the impacts that follow for the organization.
questions.pre_read: Note what the assessment's ratings measure before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Privacy risk is the chance that people suffer problems from how their data is processed. Showing members' location to their matches could lead to stalking or physical harm; fines and press coverage are costs that follow for the service. Rating harm to members first, then the service's impacts, shows the owner the real exposure. Counting members who leave is the runner-up: it is one more cost to the service and still omits the harm.

wrong_explanations.A: Sharper fine estimates refine the same narrow measure; a feature can be lawful and still expose members to stalking, which no fine figure captures.
wrong_explanations.B: The harm comes from the feature working as designed; a penetration test looks for security flaws, not the risk of showing members' location.
wrong_explanations.C: Members leaving is a cost to the service that follows from harm; adding it keeps every rating on the service's losses and still omits the harm to members.

tips: Eliminate: A sharpens the fine estimates the ratings already use, and B tests for security flaws when the harm comes from the feature working as designed.
Final two: D beats C because members leaving is still a cost to the service; a privacy assessment rates the problems for the people first, then the costs that follow.
Exam cue: privacy risk starts with the people whose data is processed; fines, lost customers and press coverage follow from their harm.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. What Zero Trust access changes
questions.question: A courier firm's depot applications now sit behind tested Zero Trust access that checks the user and device in each session. Which register scenario's rating should the risk practitioner expect to fall MOST?

options.A: An intruder using one stolen login to reach other systems
options.B: A driver misusing customer addresses within their job access
options.C: A cloud outage taking the depot applications offline
options.D: Depot staff mistyping parcel details that misroute deliveries

questions.key_concept: Zero Trust removes trust based on network location, so its largest effect is on lateral movement from a compromised account or device.
questions.pre_read: Match each scenario to the kind of control that would change its likelihood or impact.
questions.correct_explanation: Zero Trust grants no trust for network location and checks the user and device in each session, so an intruder with one stolen login can no longer move freely from system to system; NIST SP 800-207 says this stops compromised accounts moving laterally. A driver misusing permitted addresses is the runner-up: the checks confirm a valid driver on a valid device, so access the job grants is still allowed.

wrong_explanations.B: Per-session checks confirm a valid driver on a valid device; misuse of addresses the job allows passes them, so this rating moves little.
wrong_explanations.C: Zero Trust governs who may connect, not whether the cloud service runs; its policy service can even add a dependency for availability.
wrong_explanations.D: Typing errors by authorized staff happen inside permitted access; input checks, not access decisions, change this rating.

tips: Eliminate: C is an availability event that access checks cannot prevent, and D is an error by authorized staff that input controls, not access decisions, address.
Final two: A beats B because a valid driver on a valid device passes every check, while a stolen login can no longer move freely from system to system.
Exam cue: Zero Trust cuts the reach of a compromised account or device; it does little against outages, honest errors or misuse within granted access.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Unpatched controllers awaiting replacement
questions.question: A semiconductor fab's lithography controllers run an operating system that the vendor no longer patches. Replacement is due in 2029, and the analyzed risk is above appetite. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Acceptance of the risk by the lithography process owner
options.B: Vulnerability scans of the controllers, reported to the process owner
options.C: Isolation of the controllers on a separate network segment
options.D: A request that the process owner raise the risk appetite

questions.key_concept: Unpatchable legacy technology needs a compensating control, such as isolation, until replacement; finding flaws no one can fix lowers nothing.
questions.pre_read: Note where the rating sits against appetite and what the vendor still provides.
questions.correct_explanation: With no patches coming and replacement years away, the risk above appetite must be treated now. Isolating the controllers on a separate segment removes most routes an attacker could use to reach them; NIST SP 800-53 SA-22 names isolation as a way to reduce the risk of unsupported components. Vulnerability scans are the runner-up: they show which flaws exist, but none can be patched, so the exposure stays above appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: An owner may accept risk within appetite; this rating is above it, so the process owner cannot accept it, and the exposure would continue as it is.
wrong_explanations.B: Scans list the controllers' flaws, but the vendor issues no patches, so the findings cannot be fixed and the exposure stays where it is.
wrong_explanations.D: Senior management and the board set risk appetite; a process owner cannot raise it, and loosening the limit to fit one risk does not reduce that risk.

tips: Eliminate: A and D both turn to the process owner, who can accept only risk within appetite and cannot change appetite, which senior management and the board set.
Final two: C beats B because scans find flaws that no patch will fix, while isolation cuts the routes an attacker would use until the 2029 replacement.
Exam cue: when legacy technology cannot be patched and its risk is above appetite, look for a compensating control that reduces exposure, not more ways to watch it.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. An AI coding agent in the build pipeline
questions.question: A credit bureau's build pipeline lets an AI coding agent write fixes for failed builds, then merge and deploy each fix itself once the automated tests pass. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Weekly review of the agent's merged fixes by the service owner
options.B: More automated tests that each agent fix must pass
options.C: An engineer's approval before each agent fix is merged
options.D: Removal of the agent from the build pipeline

questions.key_concept: Separation of duties in a pipeline covers AI agents: a change an agent writes still needs approval by someone else before it is merged.
questions.pre_read: Trace one fix from the failed build to production before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: When the agent merges its own fixes, the same actor writes and approves each change, so passing tests are the only check. An engineer's approval before each merge restores separation of duties in the pipeline, as for code people write. A weekly review by the service owner is the runner-up: it is a real check, but it comes after the fixes are merged and released, when a faulty or unsafe change may already be running.

wrong_explanations.A: A weekly review finds problems only after the fixes are merged and released, so a faulty or unsafe change can run in production for days first.
wrong_explanations.B: More tests widen what the agent's fixes must pass, but the agent still approves its own changes, and tests check only what they were written to check.
wrong_explanations.D: Removing the agent gives up its benefit when an approval step can control the risk; banning a new tool outright is rarely the proportionate response.

tips: Eliminate: B adds tests yet leaves the agent approving its own changes, and D bans a useful tool when an approval step can control the risk.
Final two: C beats A because approval before merging stops a bad fix reaching production; a weekly review finds it only after it has run.
Exam cue: separation of duties applies to AI agents too; whoever, or whatever, writes a change should not be the one that approves it.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). One password across every unit
questions.question: A medical device maker's infusion pump design gives every unit the same administrator password, and the draft manual tells hospitals to change it at setup. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A longer shared pump password chosen by the product owner
options.B: Training for hospital staff on changing it at setup
options.C: A risk owner's contract term making hospitals liable
options.D: A unique password set on each pump at the factory

questions.key_concept: Secure settings belong in the design by default; relying on each customer to change a shared default password leaves units exposed.
questions.pre_read: Note who must act for the design to be safe, and what happens when one of them does not.
questions.correct_explanation: One password shared by every pump means a single leak exposes every unit whose hospital skipped the change, and the design relies on each customer to act. Setting a unique password on each pump at the factory removes the shared secret at the source. Training hospital staff is the runner-up: it raises how many hospitals change the password, but any that miss the step still leave pumps open to anyone who knows it.

wrong_explanations.A: A longer password is harder to guess but is still one secret shared by every pump; once it leaks or is published, every unchanged unit is open.
wrong_explanations.B: Training helps more hospitals make the change, but security that depends on every customer acting leaves pumps exposed wherever one step is missed.
wrong_explanations.C: Shifting liability to hospitals moves cost, not the hazard; patients are still at risk from pumps that anyone with the shared password can reach.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps one secret shared across every pump, and C shifts liability while the hazard to patients stays.
Final two: D beats B because a unique factory password removes the shared secret by design; training still relies on each hospital acting.
Exam cue: when a design leaves a security step to every customer, prefer the option that makes the default secure before the product ships.

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Clicks falling on reused lures
questions.question: A zipper maker's phishing simulations reuse the same five lure templates. Clicks fell from 20% to 3%, and the security manager reports staff awareness as fixed. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Further training for the staff who clicked on the lures
options.B: Fresh lures of difficulty comparable to earlier ones
options.C: Report rates tracked alongside the click rates
options.D: Review of the content in the awareness course

questions.key_concept: An awareness result counts when the test stays comparable; reused lures measure memory of the templates, so fresh lures of similar difficulty are needed.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the falling click rate could be measuring besides awareness.
questions.correct_explanation: Reusing five templates lets staff learn the lures themselves, so the fall from 20% to 3% may show recognition of those emails rather than better judgment of real phishing. Fresh lures of comparable difficulty keep the trend comparable while testing whether staff spot phishing they have not seen. Report rates are the runner-up: reporting is a better behavior measure, but staff can report familiar templates as easily, so the reused lures inflate it too.

wrong_explanations.A: With clicks at 3%, more training for a few staff leaves the question open: the drop may reflect familiarity with five reused templates, not better judgment.
wrong_explanations.C: Report rates measure behavior better than clicks, but staff who recognize a reused template can report it as easily, so the same five lures inflate both figures.
wrong_explanations.D: Nothing points to a fault in the course; the doubt is whether simulations reusing five templates still measure how staff handle real phishing.

tips: Eliminate: A trains the few who clicked and D reviews a course nothing faults; neither tells whether the fall to 3% reflects better judgment or familiar templates.
Final two: B beats C because the same five templates are reused; report rates are a better measure, but familiar lures inflate them too, while fresh lures test real judgment.
Exam cue: before crediting an improving awareness figure, check whether the test has grown familiar; compare results on fresh tests of similar difficulty.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Starting a post-quantum move
questions.question: An invoice finance firm's CIO wants the post-quantum move to start with the customer portal, the firm's most visible system. No record shows which systems use quantum-vulnerable algorithms. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Cryptographic inventory of the systems and the data they protect
options.B: Migration order set by how long the systems' data must stay secret
options.C: Post-quantum algorithms on the customer portal, as planned
options.D: A gateway its vendor says makes old algorithms quantum-safe

questions.key_concept: With no record of where quantum-vulnerable algorithms are used, post-quantum migration starts with a cryptographic inventory; ranking by how long data must stay secret follows.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the firm has no record of, and what each option assumes.
questions.correct_explanation: No record shows where quantum-vulnerable algorithms are used, so neither the CIO's plan nor any other order can be judged against the firm's real exposure. An inventory of the systems and the data those algorithms protect comes first, as NIST's transition guidance advises. Ordering by how long each system's data must stay secret is the runner-up: it is how migration is prioritized, but it needs to know which systems use vulnerable algorithms first.

wrong_explanations.B: Ordering by how long data must stay secret is how migration is prioritized, but it needs the inventory first; no record shows which systems use vulnerable algorithms.
wrong_explanations.C: Starting with the most visible system orders the move by appearance, not exposure; without an inventory, the portal may not be where long-lived data is at risk.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor's quantum-safe claim is unverified, and a gateway covers traffic through it, not systems nobody has listed.

tips: Eliminate: C picks the first system by visibility, and D relies on a vendor's quantum-safe claim; neither starts from knowing where vulnerable algorithms protect data.
Final two: A beats B because no record shows which systems use vulnerable algorithms; ranking by how long data must stay secret comes once the inventory exists.
Exam cue: when a post-quantum move is planned with no record of where vulnerable algorithms are used, recommend the cryptographic inventory first; prioritizing by data lifetime comes next.

questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. One administrator holding a master key
questions.question: One IT administrator at an ink maker can obtain and use the master key to its encrypted formula archive without anyone else. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A renewed background check on the IT administrator
options.B: A tamper-evident log of who uses the master key
options.C: Backup copy of the master key held in a separate secure location
options.D: Two-person control over retrieving and using the master key

questions.key_concept: When one person can obtain and use a key to critical data alone, two-person control applies separation of duties, so key use needs two people.
questions.pre_read: Note what one person can do with the key, and what each option changes about that.
questions.correct_explanation: One administrator can obtain and use the key to the formula archive with no one else involved, so a single person could decrypt and copy the formulas. Two-person control applies separation of duties to the key: retrieving and using it needs a second person, stopping misuse by one. A tamper-evident log is the runner-up: it records each use, but it reveals misuse after the formulas are copied, and a leaked formula cannot be recalled.

wrong_explanations.A: Screening lowers the chance of hiring someone untrustworthy, but trusted people can still misuse access; the administrator could still use the key with no one else involved.
wrong_explanations.B: A tamper-evident log detects misuse after it happens; it does not stop one administrator decrypting and copying the formulas, which cannot be recalled once leaked.
wrong_explanations.C: A second copy guards against losing the key, not against misuse; it adds another place the key can be taken from.

tips: Eliminate: A screens the person and C keeps a spare key elsewhere; neither stops one administrator from using the key with no one else involved.
Final two: D beats B because a log shows misuse after the formulas are copied, while two-person control needs a second person before the key can be used.
Exam cue: when one person can obtain and use the key to a critical asset with no one else involved, apply separation of duties to the key through two-person control, not logs.
